speechtext:
In a few words I wish to support the resolution, speaking as a member from British Columbia. I cannot add anything to what has already been said in dtescribing the necessity for the project. This necessity was well stated' this afternoon by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) and others, but I must say that I do not quite agree with the approach of the hon. and gallant member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt). The argument he put forward in connection with the necessity for this railroad extension seemed to me to imply that it was for the advancement and building up of Vancouver.
Personally I think that is a wrong approach to the situation. I always rise to the bait, so to speak, when I hear people glorifying cities and size, and now I am making a countryman's protest. I think the railway should be built, just as other services should be provided, for the building up of smaller districts and not for the purpose of making cities larger. The object should be to decentralize our economy.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard also suggested that Vancouver was one of the leading mining cities in Canada. So far as I know, all mining that has been done in Vancouver has been done on paper. These facilities, railways and roads, are necessary to decentralize our economy and build up the small communities that are the strength and the bright spots in our present democracy.
Take British Columbia. You do not go to Vancouver to see democracy at its best, but to Nelson, Penticton, Kelowna, Kamloops and Chilliwack. We must emphasize the development of these backwoods districts, this hinterland, and not build railways with the idea of simply making larger the cities that are already oversize.
There are on the order paper five resolutions dealing with essential developments in Canada to-day. Personally, I think this is absolutely unnecesssary. This method of approach is

Peace River-Railway Outlet
entirely obsolete. Why are we following such a method? We have to do so at present because no other approach is possible for members of the opposition. We are doing so because the government has failed to bring down a plan for reconstruction covering Canada as a whole. Instead of private members rising to support a railway here, a road there, a bridge here and a wateway there, the government, in my opinion, should have produced an over-all plan, a five-year plan if you like, for reconstruction throughout Canada, having in view tihe necessities of all sections, and then we would discuss it as a Canadian project and not as so many provincial or community understakings. Then we would have railways and roads proposed for British Columbia, irrigation projects for the prairie provinces, waterways for possibly Ontario and Quebec, and coastal facilities for the maritimes.	[DOT]
I trust that this policy of bits and bobs will soon be done away with and that we shall stream-line our procedure for the future, bringing in a plan covering a period of years to take care of the economic necessities of the country as a whole.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order that the members from British Columbia may be unanimous in their endorsation of the resolution moved by the hon member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine), I should like to voice my support for his proposal, and also to congratulate him on the able manner in which he presented the facts of the case. I sincerely trust the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) is not going to be too well informed, so that he may be able to change our minds on the subject.
There is, it appears to me, one very .important matter which has not been brought out to-day, a matter which the minister, who is from the east, may not appreciate. It is that I was going to say most but I will say many of the intelligent people of Canada are moving to the Pacific coast, and we in British Columbia are not able to support these people in our large urban areas, so that we must develop our outlying country, our hinterland. If we in British Columbia are to take care of the population which is going to crowd into that province, we shall have to open up our backwoods, where our great natural wealth lies. So that I would ask the minister to give this matter serious consideration and to do everything he possibly can to forward this project.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is really a matter of some concern to a minister of the crown when everyone in the house is of the same mind in regard to a project of such importance.
I make that statement deliberately, because as a rule the house is in disagreement on matters that are brought forward. As I note the temper of the house in regard to this resolution, I recall the statement made by a former member of this house some years ago, that when the house agrees upon an important project, generally the house is wrong.
Whether or not that be so, it is not my intention this evening to oppose the resolution. Before I go on to discuss it I think I should congratulate the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) on the manner in which he brought the resolution forward. I think he deserves the commendation of hon. members generally for the fair way in which he presented the matter. I think, too, I should add a word of commendation to those who have joined in the debate. It is always pleasing when a subject is discussed in such a non-partisan way, and I think what I have said applies to all who have taken part in this discussion.
In saying what I have to say on this subject this evening I should like the hon. gentleman who introduced the resolution to understand that I am not opposing it. I feel sympathetic toward him and toward the plight in which the people in the Peace River block find themselves but at the moment I am simply discussing the resolution, pointing out some of the objections and some of the difficulties that lie in the way. That there are some objections and difficulties is beyond question, though with many things said by the hon. gentleman I find myself in complete agreement. With others I find that I must disagree, and with those I shall deal at greater length a little later on.
A great deal has been said this evening about the matter of cost. Whether or not hon. gentlemen like it, whether we have in mind a private railway or a public railway, the cost factor must enter into the picture. I make that general statement now, and will come back to it a little later oh. The problem which has been discussed this evening, that of providing an outlet from the Peace River block to the Pacific seaboard, is not new; it has been discussed in this house for many years. It has been the subject of discussion among agriculturists, ranchers, mining engineers, railway engineers, government officials and the like for more than a quarter of a century. During all that time the complaint has been that people living in the Peace River
Peace River-Railway Outlet

block have to back-track or back-haul some five hundred miles before they can reroute their products to the relatively near ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert. That backhaul is necessary because a chain of mountains intervenes between the seaboard and the Peace River area. The existing railway facilities in the area consist of the Northern Alberta railways, owned and operated jointly by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The distance from railhead at Dawson Creek, British Columbia, to Edmonton, Alberta, is some 500 miles; and the farmers, ranchers and others complain with some degree of equity and justice that they have to reroute their products back in the direction of Edmonton before they can go on to the closer ports on the Pacific coast.
On going over the debates of the house, I find that almost every year from 1922 to 1933 a resolution similar to that before the house this evening was placed on the order paper and debated exhaustively. This evening the hon. member for Cariboo has brought forward the arguments which militate in favour of the construction of this railway. In doing so, [DOT] however, he has raised a very important point, which must come to the attention of the house sooner or later. It is that the policy in reference to the construction of new lines, branch lines or the extension of lines must receive consideration by parliament at some time or another; and in that respect I have to remind the house of the statement made the other evening by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe). The minister dealt extensively with economic conditions in Canada at the moment. One of the things he said was that if at the beginning of the war he had been told that steel production in Canada would have doubled during the war years, he would not have believed it. Then he said that riot only had it doubled but that in the last six months steel production has been in short supply and that there is a backlog of requirements which makes the position very difficult. In view of the statement of the minister that steel is in short supply, of necessity one must have that in mind in dealing with the "immediate consideration" referred to in the resolution.
Then the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply went on to refer to the housing situation, and to say how vital a problem housing is in Canada at the present time. Everyone in this house knows that steel will be in great demand in connection with the construction of commercial buildings and housing generally. Then there is the all-important point of cost'. Hon. members in their discussion this afternoon seemed to put that to

one side, and say -that the time had come when railways of this kind could be built regardless of cost. I say to the house this, that I have before me at the present time some twenty applications from bodies all across Canada demanding the construction of railway lines. The people who have put forward, these requests think them reasonable, and all think they should be built without delay. Some of those lines would be unprofitable, by any stretch of the imagination; others would not even begin to pay operating costs, and still others would npt pay operating costs until they had been in existence or in operation for many years. Some, too, might well be profitable.
Therefore I say to the hon. member that the question of cost, notwithstanding what has been said in the house, is not the allimportant factor, but it is certainly a factor which must be taken into consideration. Whether a railway costs $1 million or $100 million is a matter in which certainly the Minister of Finance would be interested because, particularly during the debate on the speech from the throne at this session, there has been an all-out demand for the retrenchment of expenditures. On Friday of last week the Minister of Finance was able to bring down estimates in which he showed a substantial reduction in expenditures.
I must remind the house that we cannot have the expenditures, and at the same time have the reduction in taxation. There is in the house a demand for a reduction in taxation. I believe there are on the order paper resolutions to that effect. I believe there is, too, on the order paper a resolution to the effect that exemption from taxation should be increased in the case of single men, and in the case of married men as well.
The point I wish to make is this. In a matter of this kind cost is a factor which unquestionably must be taken into consideration. Then, again, when the general question is considered, namely that in which I have just been engaged -the short supply of steel, the extreme necessity for housing, the question of curtailing expenditures and reducing taxes-it may well be that the building of railways will have to await a betterment in the position of those three items.
I note that one hon. member said this should be considered as a great post-war project. Perhaps that is somewhat in contradiction of the resolution, which demands immediate consideration. Having made those general observations, I should like now to address myself to the subject matter of the resolution in particular.

Peace River-Railway Outlet
Again I say to him this, I am not opposing his resolution; I am discussing it, and pointing to some of the difficulties which lie in the way. The difficulties as I see them are three in number. They are physiographic, economic and financial.
Four routes have been discussed as possible solutions to the Peace River area. They are, first the Aggie-Obed outlet, which was mentioned in one of the reports of the commission. Next is the Monkman pass route; the third is Pine pass route, and the fourth is the Peace River route. Any one of these routes would provide an outlet from the territory under discussion; and any one of them would, I take it, meet with the approval of hon. members, although I note that some preference has been indicated in favour of one or other of the four routes.
Since 1925 a number of surveys have been made by the government in connection with these various routes. In these surveys the government has sought to obtain from engineers, who are experts in the matter, who know their business, and who have given the matter some study, various opinions respecting the four routes.
I am informed that five such surveys were made, over the course of the years, and I should like to deal with those surveys as briefly as possible. The first of them was made in 1925, jointly by the Canadian National Railways .and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The report was tabled in the house in 1927. That report went fully into the cost, the economics, the facilities, the transportation, and the branch lines which would be required if any one of these branch routes was proceeded with by the government.
The economic studies of the engineers in this report indicated that the best possible route at that time was the Aggie-Obed route, because it was the shortest, and because also is connected the line of the Northern Alberta railroad with the Canadian National Railways at Obed.
Another question, too, was considered in the report, namely as to whether Vancouver or Prince Rupert should be the objective of the western outlet. It was considered that the former port would attract most of the business for many years to come, certainly for such a period as would make it unnecessary to consider any other alternative. The engineers estimated that the minimum cost of the Aggie-Obed route would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of S13 million. They estimated further that the maximum cost would be over $80 million.
The report went on to say, too, that when the traffic out of the Peace River district had reached the amount of over $1,080,000 tons, there should be considered the possibility or the practicability of building the outlet.
I should like to put on record the conclusions of the report. I now quote from the report on various proposed railway routes for a western outlet to the Pacific from the Peace River district, by a joint board of engineers of the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company, dated 1926 and 1927:
We may therefore briefly sum up. the results of our studies in the following conclusions:
(1)	The route via Obed is the best western outlet to the Pacific, that is from the national standpoint or from the standpoint of the Canadian National Railways. It may not be the best from the standpoint of the Canadian Pacific Railway, as it implies using part of the Canadian National Railways lines.
(2)	The immediate minimum outlay will be $13,336,000.
(3)	To fully develop the section we have considered will require a minimum outlay of over $80, million, and this does not include any betterments on existing roadways.
(4)	There is no hope even with the existing freight rate of about 39 cents per 100 pounds, for the line to pay even operating expenses on the immediate traffic, or on a traffic many times the present traffic.
(5)	There seems little hope of the line ever being self-supporting -at rates even 50 per cent higher than the present ton-mile freight rate on grain to Fort William for similar distance.
(6)	It would be more economical to handle the business, regardless of the rate received, over the existing lines until the traffic was many times the present.
So much for the joint report of 1925. The next report was that of 1929-30. This was made at the instance of the British Columbia government in cooperation with the railway. The report is not in the Department of Transport; I have not seen it and therefore I am unable to discuss it.
The third report, made in 1931, was made by the engineers of the Canadian Pacific railway at a cost of $250,000 to that railway. It did not agree with the report of 1925 which had recommended the Aggie-Obed route; it rather favoured the Peace river route. The report then went on to say that in the opinion of the engineers, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company favoured a northern route, the Peace River pass.
When that report was brought to the attention of the then Minister of Railways and Canals he tried to get the two railways to agree on a route. He brought them into his office, but all he was able to get the railways to agree upon at that time was that neither of tihe railways should build the outlet but that the government of Canada should foot

Peace River-Railway Outlet

the bill. I do not know what the position of the railways would be to-day with reference to that point, but I have no reason to believe that it would be any different in 1946 from what it was in 1931.
The fourth report, made in 1932, was made jointly by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and is known as the Crysdale report. It again went into the various routes, and again this joint report recommended the Aggie-Obed route as being the best outlet to the Pacific coast. That report differs very little from any of those I have discussed up to the moment. I should like to summarize the report by reading the concluding remarks which I think are very much to the point. I am quoting from the Peace River outlet report by the committee of railway engineers appointed to consider the matter in 1931:
At the time the 1925 report was made, local interests were mainly concerned in obtaining a western outlet to cheapen their freight cost to the Pacific, 'and supply further railway mileage in the district. Since that time, a reduction of freight rates has been accorded them, now substantially equalling rates which would obtain if a western outlet were in use.
I pause here a moment because I think the hon. member for Cariboo by his statement would lead the house to believe-at least I gathered his meaning to be such-that the people living in the Peace River area were in a difficult position because they had to pay higher rates on account of the five hundred miles over which they had to back-haul their products before they could again be rerouted to the Pacific coast. I understood him to say that for that reason the freight rate was higher than it would normally be, but I am informed that such is not the case. Certainly that is not the conclusion I have just referred to. In order to make sure that I was not misinformed I got from the officers of the Canadian National Railways a statement on that point.
I am informed that in 1926 the railways voluntarily applied for preferential rates on wheat and wheat products, moving from the Peace River area to the Pacific coast. Those rates were put into effect and have been maintained ever since. They were so favourable that the establishment of the Crowsnest pass rates in 1928 had no effect on the preferential rates. For example, a movement from Grande Prairie to Vancouver under the rates existing prior to 1926 would carry a rate of forty-one 3ents a hundred pounds. The preferential rate was twenty-eight cents a hundred pounds. If the Obed cut-off were provided, shippers in the Peace river area would get a benefit of

only about two cents a hundred pound. I now come back to the conclusion of the report of 1932, which is:
Thus, if not all, have the main requirements of the local interest been met. As the development of the district is from time to time pushed beyond reasonable road haulage distance from the existing lines of railways, local interest will demand further railway mileage. In our opinion this can be, as and when necessary, readily met by further branch-line construction.
In view of the above, our conclusions are:
1.	No western outlet is justified for the present, as the existing railway furnishes the most economical route. It will take many times the present traffic to justify another railway outlet.
2.	The Obed route for a western outlet is the
most favourable from a railway economic standpoint, considering the present phase of the railway situation.	.
3.	We recommend that the matter of a final route be decided when the question is a practical one, believing that by the time the volume of traffic has reached a point where the western outlet is justified, general and possible local conditions may have materially changed. When the decision is imperative, the whole situation should be reviewed, in order to appraise all the contributing factors, including the potential traffic which may accrue from the lands beyond the definite areas included in this report.
I point to this fact because I want to come back to it in a moment. It is concluded here that when the question of building a route becomes practicable, it should receive the attention of the railway. On the files of the department are two letters concerning this report which I think might interest the house. One of these letters was written by Sir Henry Thornton, then president of Canadian National Railways. The other was written by Sir Edward Beatty, who at that time was president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Notwithstanding the report of the joint engineers recommending the Aggie-Obed route, Sir Henry Thornton wrote to the then Minister of Railways and Canals indicating that he favoured the Obed outlet above everything else but that he did not regard that outlet as a western route. He regarded it rather as a southern outlet, the grades being better than through the Monkman pass and construction being much less costly.
Sir Edward Beatty, on the other hand, endorsed the general conclusion of the joint report with but one exception, that exception relating to the Obed route. He favoured the Peace river route because he believed that the Peace River outlet must be justified on its own permanent value. He stated that while the Obed route was the cheaper of the two from the point of view of construction costs, it could not be considered a proper solution of
Peace River-Railway Outlet
the question because in his estimation the Peace river route, tapping as it did northern resources, was the better of the two.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: In what year were those two letters written?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I have them in my office. Speaking from memory they were written shortly after the Crysdale report.
That brings me to the point I mentioned a moment ago:	Is the question of building
an outlet from the Peace River block to the Pacific coast a practical one to-day? Is tlhat not the question which, above all else, would interest the house? Is the project a practical one from the point of view of cost, from the point of view of population, from the point of view of traffic and from several other points of view? I am sure the house would not want the government to undertake a project of this kind if it we;e convinced that it was not a practical one from those points of view. That is the question which must be considered in the light of the reports, and I should like to deal with it for two or three minutes before I go on to the final report, which was brought down this year and which, I have to say, does not differ a great deal from the reports of 1925, 1931 and 1932.
The question of whether or not the line is practical is one which should engage the attention of the house before a project of this kind is advanced any further.
The house will remember that the joint report of 1925 estimated that when the traffic on the road amounted to 1,080,000 tons it would be economical to build the Aggie-Obed outlet. The figures which I have before me at the moment, and which I should like to give to the house, indicate that with the exception of the war years the traffic over the route for the past ten years has been nowhere near
1,000,000 tons.
I have before me a statement prepared by the Department of Transport on the Northern Alberta Railways. It has to do with the total tonnage carried over these railways from 1932 to 1945 inclusive. In 1932 the total freight tonnage carried over the Northern Alberta Railways amounted to 525,000 tons; 1935,
451.000	tons; 1939, 533,000 tons; 1941. 721,000 tons; 1943, 1,307,000 tons; 1944, 1,345,000 tons; 1945, 959,000 tons. That is the total traffic carried over the Northern Alberta Railways. How much of that traffic comes from the Peace River area I am not able to say, but we all know that a great deal of the traffic over the Northern Alberta Railways goes to Waterways and on to the Mackenzie river district. It is 63260-301
estimated, although I have no manner of proving this statement, by the officers of the Department of Transport that there would have emanated from the Peace River block some 250.000 tons of freight going over the Northern Alberta Railways. If that is the case, we are far from the 1.080,000 tons mentioned in the report of 1925.
While on that subject, may I take one minute of the time of the house to give the operating surplus or deficit of the Northern Alberta Railways for the period from 1932 to 1945. In each year the operating deficit was $1,000,000 or more, with the exception of 1942 and 1943, when the surplus was $1-3 million and $2-5 million. I mention that because it is a factor which must be taken into consideration. The house knows that the operating deficit on the Hudson Bay railway each year amounts to almost half a million dollars and sometimes more than that. Over and above that, there is the cost of the capital construction, which amounts to from $30,(XX),000 to $35,000,000. If the interest thereon were added to the operating deficit on the Hudson Bay railway it would make a total deficit, operating and construction, of about $1,500,000 a year.
The point I make is that if on the Northern Alberta Railways there has been a yearly deficit of almost $1,000,000, what then would be the deficit on the Peace River outlet if it were built?
I now come to the fifth report. It is known as the province of British Columbia report of the committee on resources and railways, 1945. Early in 1945 the government of British Columbia advised this government that it intended to set up a joint committee with the Canadian National Railways to study railway locations and railway lines in northern British Columbia, and it asked this government to appoint members to that committee. The government consented to send two delegates, one representing the Department of Transport and one the Canadian National Railways and it gave these two delegates certain instructions. That committee met on several occasions and finally made itd report, which I have before me at the moment. The conclusions of this report are not a great deal different from those of the previous reports, but there are a number of interesting things in this report to which I think the house would like to have me refer not only because they rave a close bearing on the whole subject-matter of the hon. member's resolution but also because they look at the matter from perhaps a little different aspect. They consider the problem from the point of view of the Pacific Great

Peace River-Railway Outlet
Eastern. I do not know what the views of the two great provinces interested in this project are in this respect, but I would take it that Alberta would be far more interested in developing the Northern Alberta Railways onward from Hines Creek and Dawson Creek, and across to Hudson Hope and Finlay Forks, than in extending the P.G.E. from either Squamish to Vancouver or from Quesnel to Prince George.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: If the railway is extended from Dawson Creek, where would it pass the Peace? At Hudson Hope? There is a splendid position at Hudson Hope.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Yes; I intend to deal with that more fully in a moment.
I go on to the report of 1945, and I see in it a number of things which I think cannot do other than commend themselves to the attention of the house. One of the conclusions we find in it is that it is essential to the proper development of a pioneer country that rail and highway facilities be coordinated. That is extremely important. Railway engineers, I think, are coming to the conclusion that it is far cheaper to coordinate rail and highway facilities than to build railways or even to extend branch lines.
Then this report approves the Peace River outlet. It agrees that the Peace River route is strategically and fundamentally the route by which the northern resources of this great country can be tapped; and here, when it refers to the great natural resources in northern British Columbia and northern Alberta, I cannot but find myself in agreement with my hon. friend; I agree with everything he said in that statement. I myself was amazed to see w'hat immense wealth there is in that great country. It is a potential reservoir of natural resources. There is practically everything there. There are forests and fisheries; there is agriculture; there is mineral wealth of all kinds; there is gold, silver, lead, zinc, uranium.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Coal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
There is coal in large quantities. My hon. friend has referred to the coal deposits-and so has the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol)-the centre of which is at Hudson Hope; and someone, I believe, has compared it with the deposits of the whole of the North American continent. I believe that statements of that kind are verified in this report. There can be no doubt about the immense natural wealth of that country. The climate, too, is extremely favourable. It is said in this report that the natives and people living there are able to 
have gardens and grow vegetables and even berries at certain seasons of the year, which would indicate that the territory can be easily inhabited. But the report states, too, that the extension from Prince George n-orth to Hudson Hope will mot improve 'the balance sheet of the Pacific Great Eastern as a whole until the density of traffic has reached 1,000,000 tons; and here we have in 1945 a report which agrees almost in its entirety with that of 1925, twenty years previously; namely, it lays stress on the fact that until the density of traffic has reached 1,000,000 tons it will not improve the balance sheet of the P.G.E. to build the railway.
With reference to the statement made by the hon. member for Davenport that railway construction should always precede development, there are many engineers and railway economists who disagree with that statement and who say that the railway must be built after development has taken place. I am not contradicting the hon. gentleman, but I point to the statement in the report.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
The Canadian Pacific
railway went ahead of immigration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Yes; railways have gone ahead under certain circumstances, but what I am saying to the hon. member is that the statement cannot be accepted generally because some railway engineers believe there are two sides to the question. Here is what the report says. The report evades that question, but it raises this point:
The committee does not consider it within their terms of reference to state whether the extension should follow development or precede it /but whatever is decided, the need of population in the area is the problem which should receive first consideration.
That is the point which I should like to bring to the attention of the house. All through this report the question of population is the one which is emphasized, the density of traffic; and the report goes on to say that you can have all the railway facilities in the world, but unless you have the traffic you cannot have a profitable and successful railway enterprise. That truly is the point which should, I think, be brought to the attention oif the house. Again, it is said:
To obtain the full development of the resources of the country to be served by the railway directly and by its tributary highway facilities, it is necessary that the country be settled by a sufficient number of the right type of people to furnish traffic to the railway . . .
Adequately to extend the present Pacific Great Eastern to make it pay and to justify expansion of the present railway it is necessary that people move into the country and develop its natural resources.

Peace River-Railway Outlet
And again:
It must be borne in mind that facilities do not make traffic, inhabitants make traffic. There must be people to furnish goods and to provide the need for transportation. Given the people willing to pioneer, this country will support a great number in comfort.
The report concludes by saying:
The initial capital construction expenditure (of the P.G.E.) would be in the neighbourhood of $20,000,000 and there would be additonal money needed for equipment. With the present foreseeable traffic immediately available there would result an annual payment of about $1,000,000 on account of this extension. . This deficit, in a decreasing amount, would persist until the traffic volume reached approximately 1,000,000 tons a year.
I should like to conclude m5' remarks on the 1945 British Columbia report by reading the five conclusions:
1.	Keep the present Pacific Great Eastern railway where it is for the benefit of the country it serves. Coordinate bus, truck and railway services now.
2.	With the present amount of traffic in sight extension will not improve the financial balance sheet of the Pacific Great Eastern railway. A million tons a year of available railway freight would alter this conclusion.
3.	Increase the rate of settlement of the country and the rate of development of the natural resources.
4.	When justified build to Hudson Hope, a future junction of lines beyond north and south of Peace river. The southern connection with Vancouver should be altered as business warrants'.
5.	Complete and revise the railway location surveys before construction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
May I ask the minister
whether a copy of this report could be distributed to each member of the house?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I should think I have not the authority to distribute the report to the house. My understanding is that it was tabled in the legislature, and I would think there would be no difficulty in obtaining it from there. If my h.on. friend wants to see it I have no objection, but I do not think this house should table a report made to another legislature. I have not given the matter any thought, but that is how it strikes me at the moment.
I think the most important feature of this report is the recommendation to coordinate rail and highway facilities. The house may find, as time goes on, that the railway engineers will feel that rather than build lines at tremendous costs it would be much better to coordinate the existing facilities in rail and highway in order to meet requirements.
If the house will bear with me for a few moments longer I will say a word or two on the question of coordination. The out-of-line
or back-haul which is occasioned, would be a great deal less extensive by coordination as I have indicated than by the building of a new line, and that could be done by branch
lines extending westerly, aided by highway transportation, which would be capable of the development of all the natural resources of the Peace River area up to and including Hudson Hope, much more cheaply than by any other means.
With regard to the question which the hon. member for Davenport put to me, the extension of the line from Dawson Creek to Hudson Hope, thereby tapping the great coal fields of that area, that would require the construction of approximately 150 miles of line, costing probably 814 million. The construction of a through route from Hines Creek through Fort St. John on to Hudson Hope is impracticable, but a line extending seventy-five miles from Hines Creek is feasible and might cost $4,500,000. It is doubtful whether such considerable sums of money should be spent at the present time, particularly when a cheaper means of meeting all reasonable transportation requirements is available by coordination of rail and highway facilities.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: If and when the railway is constructed from Dawson Creek northwest to opposite Hudson Hope on the north side of the river, the great deposits of coal being on the north side, there will be a bridge across there and there is an excellent position for a bridge. The river is very narrow where the bridge site is, and many years ago plans were got out for it, so that the railway could go northwest from Dawson Creek, across the river at Hudson Hope direct to the coal mines. I do not like to interrupt the minister because he is doing splendidly and I must congratulate him, but I would ask him to answer the question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: This coordination provides for building both north and south of the Peace river by extension of a line from Hines creek on and the extension of the line from -Dawson Creek on and crossing the bridge over the Peace river to reach Fort St. John.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Is it suggested that the railway would run north from Dawson Creek, that is directly north, using the new United States bridge across the river? I understood the minister to say that the road would run northwest from Dawson Creek toward Hudson Hope and join the other railway if it were projected from Hines Creek toward Hudson Hope.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I hope the hon. gentleman does not get the impression that I am
Peace River-Railway Outlet

suggesting that that be done. I am discussing the coordination of the two and how it could be brought about, and I wish to discuss it in a moment with particular reference to the resolution because I think that is a matter which deserves consideration in that regard.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that the government's view is that rail and truck traffic should be coordinated?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: No, I did not say that. 1 said that certain railway economists held that view. That is not the government's view. It may or may not be.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: The minister said it was the most important thing in the report.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Yes, in this report, but this report is not the government's report. This is the report of the province of British Columbia in conjunction with the railways.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: May I ask what the government's view is, if that- is not being impertinent?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: That is what the resolution seeks. I will answer that before I sit down.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Before the minister sits down he might speak of the coordination of rail and air traffic.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, but I did not get the question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: The minister might also deal with the coordination of rail and air traffic. There seems to be rather a difference.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I am dealing with one resolution that has to do with the building of a rail outlet and not an air outlet from the Peace Rivef block, and I must address my remarks exclusively to that question. The coordination I have referred to, as applied to the resolution of the hon. member for Cariboo, would work perhaps something like this. A highway service based at Dawson Creek as railhead, not exceeding 100 miles in length of run, would serve agricultural development in the Fort St. John area lying to the west of the Beaton river. This would make use of the Alaska highway and bridge over the Peace river to reach Fort St. John. A similar service operating from railhead at Hines creek, approximately 100 miles, would develop the rest of the territory north of the Peace, and advantage might also be taken of the provincial highway toward Grimshaw to develop
(Mr. Chevrier.]
the country in that direction. If highway operations are to be conducted with an eye to economy, it would be necessary to operate with heavy trucks and trailers, and this would of necessity confine the service to main highways having adequate gravel surfac. Depots might be established along the main highways at intervals of approximately twenty miles. The railway would not attempt to render transportation service except to and from such depots.
Service via the highway could, however, be expected to develop to build a country forty miles in width and twenty miles on either side of the highway. Such service would need to be developed cooperatively with the province, which would undertake to maintain the highway in fit condition for operation and to protect the railway from unfair competition, although as regards the latter, extension of railhead would in itself largely preclude such competition.
On the other hand, the railway company would be prepared to pay standard licence fees for its motor vehicles and gasoline taxes. Highway services such as I have envisaged them would, of course, be operated at a loss, notwithstanding what has been said, and the economic advantage to which I have referred springs from the fact that the loss incurred in the highway service is less than the loss which would be incurred in railway services due in the latter case to- fixed expenses.
It follows from this that the answer to the Peace River problem might well be in the coordination of highway and railway facilities. I have dealt with the coordination of highway and railway facilities because of what is contained in this report of 1945. As I said a moment ago, it is the feeling of some railway economists who have gone into this question of the extension of the P.G.E. that such should be the policy for the future. It would remain to study the question to find out whether that policy is or is not a good one.
That brings me to the conclusion of my remarks. To sum up what I have said, the matter immediately before us is a resolution which reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to the building of a railway outlet from the Peace River country to the Pacific coiast.
I started by saying that I was not opposing the resolution, I was simply discussing it. I have pointed to some of the difficulties in the way. I have said they are three in number, physiographic, economic and financial, and I have referred also to the immediate difficulty having regard to the short supply of steel. As the resolution is worded, I can see no

Peace River-Railway Outlet
objecting to accepting it, and I now inform the house that I will ask the government to give immediate consideration to this project.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been very much gratified with the tone of the debate, which has been referred to already by the minister, and it has been a pleasure to note the general unanimity of opinion with respect to the whole question. I also appreciate very much the fact that the minister has been kind enough to accept the resolution, which as he said .means that the government will give consideration to the problem. That having been done, I desire to extend the thanks of the people I represent for the consideration the minister has given their plea, which has been presented through me.
As the minister proceeded with his remarks I made a few notes. I do not know that I shall try to go over them all, because it would take too much time; and I am afraid the order in which I have them here would not correspond with their sequence in the minister's remarks. He discussed the subject dispassionately and fairly, and there is no great objection I w'ould wish to take to what he said, certainly none at all to the attitude he adopted. But there are one or two matters upon which I should like to comment.
In the first place the minister said something as to the practicability of the construction of the road. I hope the minister has not prejudged the issue before it is considered by the government. I do not suggest that the minister said it was impractical, but there seemed some little doubt in his mind about it. In the first place, of course, I submit that it his business to be careful about everything he says on an issue as big as this, and that he and bis oolleagues must give consideration to every phase of the problem which is contained in the proposal. But I would suggest to the minister that if there is doubt as to the practicability of building the line, in my mind there is no doubt at all as to the impracticability of not building it, and I think that is of major importance at the moment.
The main questions the minister raised were: costs, the population and the traffic. The population and the traffic are practically the one question. As to costs, I do not think anyone really suggested that costs were something that could be entirely left out of consideration. Most of us realize that costs are very important matters in anything we attempt, and I do not think anyone would suggest that we should plunge into a great undertaking without carefully counting the cost. But in regard to financing the undertaking, I hope the government will not find any difficulty there if from other points of view, and especially the economic point of view, they should find its advisable to proceed with the project. It may appear to be a very big task to build this railway, but it is not such a task compared with what this government faced in 1939, the task of preparing this country for war and for the production of the materials that were necessary for the defence of this nation. That was a task which might well have staggered them. Supposing the cost of this project should go to 8100,000,000; in view of the admitted wealth of the area and the possibility of developing that wealth and using it in the national economy, surely that is not a staggering sum when we consider what may be expected from its expenditure.
Then as to the population, I would not be surprised if the population were to get less and less from now on, instead! of more and more, if the line is not built. I hazard this opinion, that it is foolish for any country to permit people to go into the backwoods without a means of transportation; and I think-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Do not talk yourself out of this. We are all with you.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
No, I am not going to do so. I am not blaming the government for having done that; as a matter of fact it has not been the general policy of this country to allow people to migrate to certain sections without building railroads to them. But certainly it is unreasonable to expect a great railway traffic when there is no railway over which the traffic can move. I think that is a reasonable thing to say; and I believe the minister will agree that if that line were built and the transportation facilities were adequate, not only would the population speedily increase, but the production of each farm unit would also increase greatly, and thus increase the traffic. May I point out to the minister that the report he gave concerning the Northern Alberta Railways very largely dealt with the years of the great depression, when practically every railroad line in Canada showed a deficit. The two years of the war period showed a marked increase in traffic, while the others, naturally, were down.
I know the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) is a very wise man, and he has given me a hint which perhaps I had better take. As I have said, I greatly appreciate the minister's attitude, but before I sit down I wish to say a word in explanation to the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl). I just want to point out that when the hon.
464	COMMONS
Social Security-Mr. Bertrand (Terrebonne)
gentleman reads my speech and his own in Hansard I think he will see that he misunderstood my point. I did not suggest that the construction of this railroad should be undertaken in order to provide employment. My suggestion was that construction of the railroad would enable us to tap the great resources of a vast territory; that new industries might well be expected to arise as a consequence, and that thereby we would be able to develop industries to meet the needs of the people, at the same time, if you like, providing employment as an incidental to the production of those goods. I wish to make it clear to my hon. friend that I have never been so foolish as to suggest a policy by which people would be provided with work merely for the pleasure of looking at them working. No one I know of has ever advocated an economic policy of that sort. Let us assume that all modern equipment is used, that we have been able even to harness atomic power, and that we have reduced the necessity of human labour to the ultimate. Still it is possible that we shall have to work for an hour or so each day. That would be full employment, under a definite set of circumstances; and that is all we mean by full employment.
Therefore I hope that with this explanation my hon. friend and I will not appear to be as far apart as one might have thought while listening to his remarks.
Motion agreed to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY ACT- ORDERS IN COUNCIL
subsubtopic: ALLOWANCES TO PERSONS SUFFERING INJURY, ACCIDENT OR CONGENITAL INFIRMITY.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should bake into consideration, the advisability of including in, their social security programme a system of allowances .to every person, without any income or means of support, who, by reason of an injury, accident or congenital infirmity, is at a disadvantage in seeking or obtaining employment, or incapable of providing for his subsistence, and whose age prevents him from benefiting by the social security legislation now in force.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution barely needs comment. Therefore my remarks will be very short because, furthermore, I should like to know the opinion of the house on this question.
The problem of social security is becoming more important than ever in a world upset by war. In this respect, Canada has accomplished an effort which deserves mentioning. Family allowances are now permitting large families with low income to face the heavy

charges imposed upon them by a higher cost of living. Indigent mothers, blind and old age people are drawing from various government grants which alleviate their sufferings and allow them an improvement in their uprooted life. Allowances and pensions afford veterans an opportunity to rebuild their civil life on a better basis, and secure them a living if, physically speaking, they have left part of themselves in this conflict. The labourer temporarily out of work may rely on unemployment insurance benefits, a social law which, however, in order to keep up with new conditions and new circumstances, should undergo several amendments.
Family allowances are stopped at the age of sixteen; old age pensions start at seventy. May I say that the age for these latter pensions should be lowered as soon as possible to sixty-five years. The 54-year difference between the ages of sixteen and seventy represents more than the average human life. In my opinion, a certain section of the people, especially included within these age limits, was left unprovided for; that is, the invalid and cripple. This group includes the victims of infantile paralysis, the victims of all kinds of accidents who do not fall under the benefits of any provincial accident insurance act, persons suffering from congenital deformity and other sick people who cannot be cured.
If they, or their famly, are wealthy, these invalids can obtain all the necessary treatments in peaceful surroundings which will thus alleviate the burden of their misfortune. If they have no money or if they are paupers, they fall under public charity. No municipal by-law will provide any help for them; no provincial law can give them any grant, and I could not discover any federal statute which could give them assistance of any kind. No one will hire any invalid person; they are not accepted on the labour market. In this age of mechanization, the machine, which does not-stop, supersedes the human being who, in order to follow it, must have strong arms, strong legs and powerful eyesight. Invalid and crippled persons are set aside for reasons of security and production. In the meantime, the cripple or invalid, out of work or occasionally employed in some casual job, cannot earn his living; if he has a wife and children, his fate is simply tragic. Then he must resort to public charity, to welfare associations, and even beg from door to door; besides his misfortune he must beg and undergo the brutal obligation of living desperate days with no hope of improvement. From week to week, under the heavy yoke he has to bear, he

Social Security-Mr. Coldwell
will become discouraged, if not filled with despair. Misfortune will poison some persons, but misery will kill him.
Crippled and invalid persons deserve their share under the sun. They have a right to happiness to the same extent as any one of us. The conditions of modem living, which are improved by scientific inventions, gives everyone a minimum of comfort. In order to win. the war, we had to spend billions; can we refuse setting aside a few hundred thousand dollars to rid us of poverty? At present we are spending millions to help the destitute populations of the old world; by an elementary sense of charity, should we not also think of those living near us who are victims of hazard, who are the outcasts of happiness?
In Great Britain, it is intended to enact-if it has not already been enacted-legislation providing for the employment of crippled and invalid persons. All employers with twenty employees or more, must hire a number of invalids equal to two per cent of their total effective. This is the disabled persons employment act. I do not know the opinion of the government over this-legislation, and even less its immediate or future intentions toward invalid or crippled persons. But I sincerely believe that, during the present session, this unfortunate section of our society should be provided for. Would it not be right for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) to study this problem, to give a statement concerning these indigent persons, and then to recommend a suitable system of allowances, paid by the federal government, or subsidized both by the federal and provincial authorities? The social security programme cannot be complete if indigent invalids and crippled persons are left to their unfortunate fate.
Everyone endorses a programme of social security for children, for the family, for indigent mothers, for the aged and blind persons and for veterans and disabled soldiers. Everyone will also endorse a movement to extend to cripples and invalids the total sympathy of the nation if special legislation to that effect is presented. Their existence on a lounge chair is restricted to the horizon of their window. They live in darkness, without life or company, in a state of perpetual restlessness toward the future, constant dejection, sleepless nights and continuous disappointment. A person who has never suffered cannot understand the darkness which is cast upon the life of a hapless person affected with infirmity, want and very often poverty. Let us brighten tiheir existence by giving them some means of living. Let us assure them that if they are
ignored locally the whole nation is not indifferent to their fate and will not reject them from our national life. Spreading joy means spreading peace. To abolish social misery means strengthening the security of the nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand! who has just introduced this resolution. I think it is worthy of the support of the house and the government. I believe the proposal that he has made to-night will before many years have passed-I was going to say I hoped before many months had passed-be given full effect.
I often think of people who are in the condition he has described, that of disability. I think of what persons with disabilities which perhaps have extended over a long period of years have to endure. That is something that those of us who enjoy good health can scarcely realize. It is all very well in the home where there is a regular income to have one who is permanently handicapped, but I often think that in homes where the income is low or where there is virtually no income the misery cannot be estimated, not only of the individual who is permanently incapacitated but of those who have to care for and see the suffering of the one afflicted.
When the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) was speaking this afternoon I thought how much we could do if we would to alleviate these chronic and, as my hon. friend has stated, congenital diseases which afflict so many persons. I know something of it myself. I wish to say that as far as the party to which I belong is concerned, for thirteen years we have urged that the aged should be cared for and that the blind should be given adequate pensions to enable them to live decently and enjoy life to the extent that they can under the circumstances from which they suffer. We have urged the same consideration for persons who suffer from arthritis and from many other diseases that are incurable, like disseminated sclerosis. I only wish that this house could see its way clear to give every sufferer who cannot earn his or her daily bread and is wholly or partly dependent on others the necessary assistance so that they may be enabled to receive the care that they should receive.
I do not want to delay the house, nor do I want to interfere with others who would like to speak to this motion before eleven o'clock. I wish again to congratulate the hon. member who introduced this resolution. I am perfectly sure that it is deserving of support. I hope we

Social Security-Mr. Marquis
shall all assist in bringing about a condition of society in which those who cannot earn their daily bread or those who are shut in and suffering may be recognized as the responsibility of the whole community. When we have achieved that I believe we shall have established the foundation of a society which may not only profess but actually become in the true sense Christian.

subsubtopic: ALLOWANCES TO PERSONS SUFFERING INJURY, ACCIDENT OR CONGENITAL INFIRMITY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not expected that this resolution would be discussed at once. I would have considered it preferable to have an opportunity of making some preparation in order to submit more adequately to this house the few arguments I have to offer. First, I wish to congratulate the mover of this resolution, the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand). He gives expression to an urgent appeal from those among the population who suffer perhaps more than any others.
We now have social laws which help children, prevent them from suffering, and ensure them food and a proper education. We have social laws whereby a helping hand is extended to old people who, after having spent the better part of their life in caring for their families and developing their country, are entitled to some compensation from the nation they have so long served. But there is one class of people who are still in a worse plight than others; I refer to those in their thirties, forties or fifties who, through some disability, are unable to earn a living. In our rural districts, I have often met some of those poor people who have aged beyond their years, and are unable to earn enough to support their wives and children, but are too proud to request any help from public organizations or municipalities or to accept any assistance from neighbours who would be in a position to help them. Those are the people who are most in need of the government's assistance.
To my mind, in keeping with the principle which made it possible for the government to pass the Old Age Pension Act, those who reach that stage prematurely, who, at fifty are as incapacitated as others are at seventy, should be entitled to state assistance.
I am happy to concur in the opinions expressed by the hon. member for Terrebonne. Twenty-five or fifty years ago, beggars could be seen everywhere in the street. Many of us as youngsters delighted in listening to some vagabond's life-story or to the tales he could tell. Nowadays, society has forged ahead and individual hardship is less frequent. Federated charities are active in our cities. This federa-

tion was inaugurated to carry on the work of essential charities and to help various associations which could not, unaided, achieve their aim.
Charity can be organized. It is not socialism but social legislation enacted in order to rectify certain anomalies and cure certain ills of our society. It is neither state paternalism for state control of individual or social groups but a remedy designed to alleviate some of our ills.
I represent a constituency whose population lives rather well and even very well, in some centres. But it has not been altogether spared. I have seen with my own eyes the head of a family dragging himself to work every day; this man should not have worked but his pride urged him to go and eke out a living for1 his wife and child, who, although she is sixteen, is herself incapable of working.
Mr. Speaker, those who have witnessed, in their own constituency or elsewhere, such cases as I have just mentioned, know that they are common to every parish, every county, every province.
In the county of Terrebonne, the citizens have urged their member to have the Old Age Pensions Act amended by parliament, for the benefit of cripples and invalids; the same request has been made in my constituency and, no doubt in others throughout the country, the same appeal has been voiced.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think this measure would impose too heavy a burden on the budget of tlhe Minister of National Health At the present time, old age pensions amount to a sizeable figure. The crippled are very much less numeapus that the old people; in fact, they constitute but an insignificant proportion of our population. Those unfortunate people are not themselves in a position to present their request, but we are by fairness and charity bound to take their interests at heart in this house.
It might be argued that the setting up of an organization for the administration of an act dealing with the invalids and the crippled would present tremendous difficulties. I would venture a suggestion in this regard. Some may think that, were we to include invalids under the old age pension act, a certain number of so-called invalids might, by playing on sentiments, obtain a certificate entitling them to benefits to which they would have no right. There is a very easy means of preventing any such fraud. Let (the Department of National Health set up a medical board, with members appointed by the government, to examine every applicant claiming to be an invalid or a cripple.

Social Security-Mr. Blackmore
Those who are really incapacitated, who are now abandoned without any government assistance, who could hardly obtain relief from municipalities or corporations, might thus be helped and assisted. Under our provincial laws, a man is not bound to help his brother. He should perhaps consider it a natural obligation, because Christianity teaches to help and to love one another. But We know that this is often forgotten, as well in mutual as in Christian love. Well, when a man has in his house one or two of his crippled brothers, he must, under Christian law, receive them and assist them, but he is not bound to do so under civil law and these disabled or incapacitated individuals are completely abandoned. Then the municipalities should offer them relief, but in many cases it is difficult to secure.
Finally, may I point out that our government has lent a helping hand to the underprivileged, protected our children and provided them with proper means of development., helping them to grow and become stronger while giving full play to their particular talents; it has also assisted the elderly, bringing a bit of happiness and comfort to them in their old age in recognition of the devoted service they rendered their country by raising a sound and strong family. I should now like to express the hope and wish that this same government will, in the near future, take the necessary steps to relieve our invalids who are unable to earn their livelihood.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I sat here to-night and heard the eloquent and beautiful expressions with which the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand) presented his case, I was unable to refrain from thinking of the vast difference which has come over the house during the last ten years. It is ten years since the members of the Social Credit group were trying to get the members of this house to listen to the idea that there should be distributed among the people purchasing power. I suppose every hon. member remembers that at that time it was a common sneer that we were advocating twenty-five dollars a month. We have all heard the hon. member for Terrebonne to-night advocate more than twenty-five dollars a month for all those who, from one cause or another, have been rendered unable to gain access to the means of life. Of course the members of the Social Credit group will endorse heartily and enthusiastically all that the hon. member for Terrebonne has said.
May I draw the attention of the house to one or two further considerations which naturally arise? The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has only just now been telling us about the need for being careful about money. The hon. member for Terrebonne is not worrying about money, and I submit Mr. Speaker, that this house must find the means of obtaining the money for the achievement of the objectives which this house finds desirable. We are living in an age of superabundance. There is no doubt whatever that we can produce all the food and clothing and shelter in this country which are necessary to provide every one of the unfortunates whom the hon. member has in mind with all he can possibly use-not a mere pittance, but an abundant life. It is equally obvious that we can produce enough to accomplish the other objectives which this house has in mind -the building of railways which will be outlets of the Peace River area, the development of other projects which will be necessary in order to make this nation strong and happy. We must find a means of turning these goods, this real wealth, into financial wealth. I would suggest that all hon. members quite earnestly set about trying to find out what that method is. With that I will close my remarks at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say only a few words in support of the motion of the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand), to tell him that his motion was due to be discussed some day, the sooner the better, and that as a medical man it is to me a pleasure and a satisfaction to give to those who are incapacitated by congenital infirmity work such as they would want to do.
I do not find, as the hon. member who has spoken before me suggests, that the chamber has changed at all. What we were discussing was not social credit, we were favouring assistance to those who could not earn their living and, as the motion of the hon. member for Terrebonne states, are without any income or means of support. If I understand well the social credit theory, its supporters want to give a bonus to everyone, incapacitated or not. That is the distinction between the social credit theory and the theory of the hon. member for Terrebonne, and that is why I am supporting the motion. As a medical man I have been very close, closer than those of any other profession, to the infirm. In my province we have hospitals and hospices to help crippled people, but even though we have these establishments I believe, with a law passed by the government adding to the social security programme, we could help the hospitals in taking care of the infirm and the crippled.

Social Security-Mr. Cote (Verdun)
That is all I have to say at this time, but I wish again to congratulate the hon. member for Terrebonne and all those who have spoken in favour of this motion.

speechtext: I just rise to congratulate. the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand) upon sponsoring this resolution and to express my hearty support of it. Some years ago, in the province of British Columbia, through regulations enacted under the jurisdiction of the social welfare department, all people coming within the scope of this resolution were cared for, on a somewhat limited basis; and then two years ago,J pending legislation by the federal government, those regulations were put into statutory form under the social assistance act. So that now, in British Columbia, by law, all people coming within the scope of this resolution are cared for in a limited manner; that is, they receive, on the whole, slightly less than those who receive old age pensions, and in British Columbia, as I think all hon. members know, $30 a month is paid to old age pensioners. While that assistance is limited and insufficient, I can speak from personal experience of what it has meant to hundreds of people in the interior of British Columbia. Even that limited assistance has changed life for them in many respects. I wish to express my support of this resolution, and I trust that all hon. members will support it and that when it is passed it will result in the federal government assuming its responsibility in this respect, and including proposals of this kind in a national security scheme which will tnake it possible for these people to live a happy and decent life.

speechtext:
I wish to join with the hon. members ^ho have congratulated the mover of this resolution. It certainly shows on his part an intention to alleviate the difficulties of those who have to compete on the labour market when handicapped by injury, accident or congenital infirmity. I am all for the help which can and should be given to that class of our Canadian population. I am just wondering what legislation in the form of concrete proposals this house could initiate without preliminary consultation with the authorities that have the prime responsibility of looking after these matters; I mean the provincial authorities. I do not know if the matter has already been the subject of any discussion at the interprovincial conference which will be resumed later on in the month, but I think this angle should have been discussed by the mover.

In the second place, I respectfully submit that before resorting to allowances and financial help to the disabled of such a category as is entitled to be covered by this resolution, all other means of rehabilitation should be resorted to. I would have preferred seeing this matter discussed under that angle. I would be a much more enthusiastic supporter of a motion which would find ways and means of rehabilitating disabled and injured persons as, for instance, the Department of Veterans Affairs does so well with the veterans of this and the other great war. Citizens of this country have a right to expect something more than charity from the government of this country. Most of them have had an active period in their life; they have contributed to the development of our economic and social life, and they are entitled to a concrete and useful help in order to reduce their disabled condition. For those disabled persons covered by this resolution who are still of an age where they can be trained in some way and rehabilitated for the labour market, I would rather suggest some ways and means of helping them to attain that end, and I would be inclined to support such a resolution as this only when I have been convinced that there was absolutely no other way of rectifying this unusual situation than by granting allowances or financial aid.
I hope that this matter will come up again for discussion in the house and that every angle of the situation will be discussed before any decision is taken. Nevertheless I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Terrebonne on having afforded the house an opportunity of discussing such an important question as help for a class of citizens who certainly cannot be left in distress and who need the assistance of the responsible authorities in the country.

speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand) on the manner in which he has introduced this resolution. I remember when the estimates of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) were before the house during the last session the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) discussed the matter rather fully, and I believe the minister said he would give sympathetic consideration to the proposals and suggestions made at that time.
As has been well pointed out by one of the speakers, it is not so serious a matter where there is a steady income, but where there is a cripple or someone who comes under any of the various headings that have been so well

Atomic Energy Commission
set forth by the hon. member, and where there are financial difficulties coupled with such incapacity, the situation is quite different.
Dealing with some of the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I would point out that there is at least one organization, and there may be more, already doing a splendid job, though it is more or less on a charitable basis. They solicit financial contributions from the public, and the last contribution I was called upon to make before coming to attend this session was solicited by such a committee. They operate two or three hospitals in the country to take care of and endeavour to train younger people, but it is most difficult for these people who find themselves in straitened circumstances financially to have to depend on such charity. If the department has not some concrete suggestion to take care of such people, as suggested by another speaker, it might well, after a thorough investigation, give some assistance to worthy institutions which are now trying on their own to assist the unfortunate who find themselves in such difficult circumstances.
If the minister will recollect the case brought forward by the hon. member for Lake Centre and other members as well when his estimates were before the house at the last session, he will recall that he said he would give the matter sympathetic consideration. I simply wished to say a few words in support of the resolution.

speechtext:
I
rise to support the motion and I am happy to see that it includes various categories. I hope it also includes those people who are suffering from arthritis and rheumatism. There are many crippling and disabling diseases that are painful. While I realize that many persons could benefit from training, I would point out that there are many others who are so incapacitated physically that it is impossible for them to use both hands, or in some other way they are incapable of engaging in any useful trade.
I hope that when the government institutes such an allowance or pension it will not wait, as in the case of pensions for the blind, until the recipient is forty years of age. It is a great mistake to leave a person to charity or chance until he or she attains that age. A pension for any of the purposes contemplated by this resolution should start where the family allowance leaves off, and we should supplement the allowance with training or some other service which would enable the individual, as far as it is humanly possible, to attain some degree of accomplishment and
human satisfaction. A great many people are handicapped and their lives unduly stunted because we have failed to make any financial provision or to give them training of any kind to develop them. I hope that the government will see fit to include such persons along with the categories set out in the dominion-provincial proposals, under which they propose to take care of certain specific diseases or disabilities. I hope also that any plans which the government has in mind will at once proceed to take care of those people who are part of our society and for whom society must take the responsibility.
